interpretation_limits: The NEA announcement confirms that the 2021-2025 hydrogeological report and a nitrate-risk field methodology were prepared; it does not expose the archive contents.
The linked RAR archive was not retrieved, hashed or inspected in this run.
No sample count, station count, analyte denominator, laboratory result, site coordinate or time-series row is asserted.

The 2026-06-24 law sets 2027-09-01 statutory milestones for relevant methodology approval and groundwater nitrate-risk-zone identification; the NEA announcement that a method was prepared does not prove formal approval or completion.

The announced report concerns groundwater monitoring and must not be merged with NFA food/drinking-water inspection records or treated as a distributed-network/bottled-water dataset without matrix confirmation.
Archive reuse and redistribution terms are not stated in the announcement and must be confirmed before publishing extracted data.
No nitrate threshold, local contamination prevalence, exposure level or public-health outcome is inferred from the announcement alone.

The WHO 2026 edition gives drinking-water guideline values of 50 mg/L as nitrate ion and 3 mg/L as nitrite ion, with a combined concentration-to-guideline ratio not exceeding 1; the chemical fact sheet lists its assessment date as 2016.
WHO guideline values are global health-based guidance, not Georgian law, and are not automatically applicable to raw groundwater unless its intended use and matrix are confirmed as drinking-water.

The WHO fact sheet identifies bottle-fed infants as the most sensitive population and notes that microbial contamination and gastrointestinal infection can increase methaemoglobinaemia risk when nitrate is present.
Excessive boiling can concentrate nitrate; boiling is not a nitrate-removal treatment.

Georgia Government Decree №58/2014 sets nitrate at 50 mg/L as NO3- and nitrite at 0.2 mg/L as NO2- for water within its scope. The WHO 2026 nitrite guideline of 3 mg/L is not a substitute for the stricter Georgian legal value.

The ENI SEIS/EEA historical baseline uses NEA data from 2016-2017: 34 of 45 groundwater monitoring sites had data, sampling was twice per year, all reported site averages were below 50 mg NO3/L, and the indicator says all except one were above 10 mg NO3/L (33/34 by subtraction).
The historical 2016-2017 indicator is not current 2026 monitoring, not a household exposure survey, and does not provide raw site/sample values or stated uncertainty.
The indicator's suggestion that lower western concentrations may relate to lower agricultural activity is a hypothesis, not a causal result.
The Georgian Decree №58/2014 general sum-of-ratios clause is not interpreted here as a specific nitrate/nitrite combined ratio without legal review.

external_drinking_water_guideline.edition_title: Guidelines for drinking-water quality: fourth edition incorporating the first, second and third addenda
external_drinking_water_guideline.interpretation: WHO health-based guidance for drinking-water: nitrate 50 mg/L as nitrate ion, nitrite 3 mg/L as nitrite ion, combined ratio <=1. Georgia Government Decree 58/2014 sets nitrate 50 mg/L as NO3- and nitrite 0.2 mg/L as NO2- for water within its scope; use the Georgian limits for legal compliance. The WHO nitrite value is not a Georgian compliance threshold and the WHO values are not automatically applicable to raw groundwater.

historical_baseline.source_publisher: ENI SEIS II East / European Environment Agency
historical_baseline.annual_mean_method: Average of annual mean groundwater nitrate concentrations for 2016-2017.
historical_baseline.sites_above_10_derivation: The indicator states that 34 sites were available and all except one had an average above 10 mg NO3/L; 34 minus 1 equals 33.
historical_baseline.regional_pattern_note: The indicator reports lower groundwater nitrate in western Georgia and suggests lower agricultural activity as a possible explanation; this is not a causal finding.
limitations: Historical data period is 2016-2017; it is not a current 2026 water-quality measurement.
Only 34 of 45 monitoring sites had data for the analysis.
Sampling frequency was twice per year; the indicator reports averages of annual means rather than every raw sample.
The page does not publish the raw site/sample values in the indicator text.
No uncertainty estimate is specified by the indicator.
The number of western sites is not stated in the page text.
Monitoring sites are not a population-weighted or household-level exposure sample.

georgian_legal_standard.scope: Natural or treated water used for drinking, food preparation, other domestic purposes, and water intended for food or food-product production.
exclusions: Water for medical or other special purposes.
An individual private source supplying less than 10 m3/day to fewer than 50 people and not connected to a commercial or public network.
Natural mineral water with total mineralization above 1500 mg/L.
georgian_legal_standard.combined_ratio_clause: Article 2(21) contains a general sum-of-ratios rule for multiple substances normalized by the same limiting sign. This record does not interpret it as a specific nitrate/nitrite combined-ratio formula; obtain legal review before applying it.
georgian_legal_standard.interpretation: Use these Georgian statutory limits for compliance when the water falls within the decree's scope. The WHO 2026 nitrite guideline value of 3 mg/L is not a substitute for Georgia's 0.2 mg/L legal limit.
